why: Shorter; cuts the backstory and anxiety narration, opens on what changed, and keeps the point without declaring feelings.
Avoids the put-down ('a guess that happens to compile') and adds the real reason, keeping the agent honest as the codebase evolves.
Cuts the trailing clause 'and it is the shape the whole map has had from the start', a low-value closer about the course itself, so the shorter version wins.
Cuts the forward hint about Module 4 and the explicit-list lesson announcement, and states the practitioner default as a plain concrete action.
B's added sentence restates the loop mechanics. Cutting a low-value sentence is the author's default call, and A reads faster.
B opens on the action ('Ask these one at a time') in fewer words. A repeats the three-questions line and tells students to watch instead of typing along, which puts them in a passive role.
Matches the author's kept text; B has the passive 'nobody can hand you', the patronizing 'gift you haven't given yet', and the duty-framed 'was never a reason to wait'.
The shorter version wins: 'Three modules in, this is your practice now' is a low-value closer and a restatement of the sentence before it.
"Read what Claude proposes" is the author's own repeated verb for this act; "Check" implies verifying all of it, and the taste rules prefer precise verbs.
The B title says the point in plain words (a check resets the chain), while A's title is a statement of the problem, and B opens on the solution the slide teaches.
Names the artefact plainly (an ADR); A's 'a future engineer can inspect' is wordier and the acronym gloss lands better with the decision framing.
Shorter header, and the body already says 'context window'; the extra word in B adds nothing.
The shorter lead-in names the action directly instead of previewing the prompt, matching the author's AE101 cut.
B makes the student passive, since which result you get depends on the session; A states it plainly and shorter.
B is shorter and drops the invented 'committed change' term for plain 'alternative'/'Alternatives'; it cuts the low-value 'gives you the floor' sentence.
The extra 'One sentence buys the time back' is a clever closer after the point is made; A is shorter.
Shorter; the closing sentence adds little once the point is made, and the author cuts such closers.
Plain bullets read faster; bolding whole lead-in sentences in B adds emphasis noise without adding information, and the text is otherwise identical.
